## ERYSIPELAS
In contrast to cellulitis, erysipelas has sharply demarcated borders and a
characteristic raised, orange-peel appearance. Most cases are associated with
streptococcus. In a minority of cases, especially those involving the face,
Staphylococcus aureus is also a potential pathogen. In severe cases,
methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) coverage must be provided
until microbiology results are available.
Treat for 5 to 10days, longer if patient is bacteremic.
## _________________________________
## Facial
## _________________________________
Sudden onset of rapidly spreading red edematous tender plaque-like skin on the
face in an otherwise healthy host.
## Inpatient

## If erysipelas-like on the face treat as if MRSA is present:
Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h ($) [R]
## _________________________________
## Non-facial
## _________________________________
## MILD TO MODERATE disease
Penicillin VK 250 - 500 mg PO q6h ($) [R]
## Alternative for penicillin allergy
Erythromycin 500 mg po q6h ($) [DI]
## SEVERE disease
Penicillin 3 million units IV q6h ($) [R]
## Alternative for penicillin allergy or MRSA suspected
Vancomycin 15 mg/kg IV q12h ($) [R]
< OR >
Clindamycin 600 mg IV q8h ($) [H,O]
## Outpatient

## If erysipelas-like on the face treat as if MRSA is present:
Refer to Inpatient Antimicrobial CDSS.
